articles.title: California man accused of making online threats against ICE agents: DOJ
articles.summary: A California man was arrested after allegedly making social media threats against ICE agents and advocating for armed attacks on government facilities.
articles.body: A California man was arrested after allegedly making social media threats against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, the Department of Justice announced on Monday. Leonard Michael Fierro, 37, of Hacienda Heights, is facing one count of interstate threats. Fierro used social media to threaten violence against ICE agents, advocate armed attacks on government facilities and encourage others to participate in a violent revolution against the U.S. government, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. "Threats of violence against federal law enforcement officers is not protected speech. They are serious criminal acts that endanger public safety and undermine the rule of law," U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. FLORIDA ATTORNEY ACCUSED OF THREATENING TO SHOOT ICE AGENTS WHILE TRYING TO BUY GUN "We will aggressively prosecute those who seek to intimidate, harm, or incite violence against the men and women who enforce our nation's laws," he continued. Last month, the FBI became aware of threatening posts allegedly made by Fierro on Instagram. In multiple posts and stories, Fierro allegedly called for an armed uprising against the U.S. government, advocated for violence against federal agents and encouraged others to join him in conducting attacks against ICE facilities. In one post, he allegedly asked followers to meet outside ICE facilities, the White House and other government buildings to "take up arms" and "overthrow" the government. Fierro also allegedly called for an armed mob to storm the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, break migrant detainees free and violently overthrow the government. Investigators also discovered that Fierro owned a firearm and had purchased approximately 700 rounds of 9mm ammunition in October and early November. He also made extensive online searches about tactical equipment, ballistic protection, surveillance countermeasures, bolt cutters, GPS tracking devices, government facilities and the Adelanto ICE detention facility, according to investigators. Fierro allegedly researched specific ICE officers and searched for information regarding a leaked database of Department of Homeland Security employees. Investigators also said he had what appeared to be a planning checklist with references to tactical gear, ammunition, GPS trackers, a rental vehicle, communication equipment and other items allegedly associated with his plot. On Nov. 5, FBI agents searched Fierro, his vehicle and his residence under judicially authorized search warrants, recovering a gun, 19 loaded magazines, more than 400 additional rounds of ammunition, tactical body armor, ballistic plates, GPS tracking devices, bolt cutters, digital devices and other equipment. Authorities later reviewed data stored on Fierro’s devices and found several videos allegedly recorded by him in late October and early November in which he discussed initiating a violent revolution, targeting ICE agents and encouraged others to conduct armed attacks against government facilities and officials. FBI ARRESTS PROTESTER WHO THREATENED TO KILL ICE OFFICER'S FAMILY AT NJ DETENTION CENTER PROTEST, BLANCHE SAYS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Investigators also recovered what appeared to be a farewell video that included Fierro talking about his anticipated death, leaving instructions for family members and saying that he expected to be found "riddled with bullet holes." Notes with Spanish-language phrases that appeared to have been made to communicate with migrant detainees during a planned attempt to free people held at an ICE detention facility were also found by investigators. If convicted, Fierro would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years behind bars. The FBI continues to investigate.

articles.title: Sundar Pichai-backed foundation's charitable grants rose from $510,000 in 2020 to nearly $9.2 million in 2025; filings show $22.9 million in distributions and a $6.16 million donor-advised fund payment
articles.summary: The Pichai Family Foundation reported nearly $9.2 million in grants during the 2025 tax year, taking its recorded charitable distributions to
articles.body: The Pichai Family Foundation reported nearly $9.2 million in grants during the 2025 tax year, taking its recorded charitable distributions to approximately $22.9 million across the tax years covered by its filings. The San Francisco-based foundation has made grants to a range of organisations since at least 2020, with its annual distributions increasing over the period. According to the foundation's 2025 Form 990-PF filing, one payment in its latest reported figures stands out: approximately $6.2 million was directed to a donor-advised fund, rather than being listed as a grant to a named charitable organisation.Sundar Pichai-backed foundation records $6.16 million against donor-advised fund in 2025The biggest payment in the 2025 list was approximately $6.16 million, recorded against GS Donor Advised Philanthropy Fund for Wealth Mgmt, based in Albany, New York. The amount accounted for roughly two-thirds of the foundation's reported grants for the year. Its stated purpose was general operating support.A donor-advised fund is a charitable giving arrangement in which money is contributed to a sponsoring organisation and placed in an account for charitable purposes. The donor can recommend grants to eligible charities over time, while the sponsoring organisation retains legal control of the assets.Where the remaining 2025 grants wentAs per the 2025 Form 990-PF filing, the foundation's other reported payments were spread across education, food assistance, healthcare, children's welfare and community organisations. Castilleja School Foundation in Palo Alto received approximately $2 million, making it the second-largest recipient in the annual list. Second Harvest of Silicon Valley was listed for about $450,000, while Boys & Girls of the Peninsula received approximately $125,000. Two international humanitarian organisations, Doctors Without Borders and UNICEF USA, were each recorded as receiving around $100,000.The same amount went to Peninsula Bridge and Pratham USA, both associated with educational initiatives. The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco received approximately $50,000, while Global Fund for Children was listed for around $25,000. A further payment of roughly $15,000 went to Aarti for Girls.The foundation reported 11 grant payments in its latest filing, with a median amount of approximately $100,000. Excluding the donor-advised fund payment, the grants ranged from around $15,000 to $2 million, with Castilleja School Foundation receiving the largest payment among the other listed organisations.How Sundar Pichai-backed foundation's charitable grants grew over five yearsThe foundation's reported grant payments have grown considerably since its earliest filing in the dataset. In 2020, it recorded seven grants worth approximately $510,000. The next available tax-year record is from 2022, when 11 payments totalled around $2.6 million. The amount rose to approximately $4.2 million in 2023, spread across 12 grants. By 2024, the foundation had reported around $6.3 million in payments through 11 grants. The 2025 figure of nearly $9.2 million represents its highest annual total in the records examined. articles.title: Turkish officials backtrack after 24-hour hunt for Istanbul lioness, saying she never existed
articles.summary: A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal did not exist.
articles.body: A 24-hour search for a lioness in the Istanbul suburbs that sparked panic among local residents was thrown into fresh confusion late Monday when Turkish officials said the animal did not exist. Istanbul’s governor mobilized teams of animal welfare experts, police and army commandos in the hunt for the lioness after it was “identified” — even releasing two videos of the animal prowling around the upmarket neighborhood of Uskumrukoy. Residents were warned to stay home, and the 54-square-kilometer (about 20 square miles) Belgrade Forest to the north of Istanbul was sealed off. By Monday evening, however, officials backtracked and said in a statement new images had been examined that showed the animal was “not a lion or any other large cat species.” “The area has been scanned from the air with a drone equipped with thermal cameras and from the ground by our teams,” the statement said. “Baiting was also carried out and motion-sensor camera traps used.” “Fieldwork has not yielded any concrete evidence of a lion being present in the area.” The abrupt change left many bewildered, wondering what animal could have been mistaken for a lioness, with some suggesting it was a large dog. Others posted mocking videos of domestic cats on social media, asking if it was the lioness. Even after the governor’s office statement, media outlets published another video of an animal emerging from bushes and asked readers if it could be a lion.

articles.title: Meta's Muse has launched in the UK. I found it helpful but awkward
articles.summary: Meta wants Muse to do for AI what WhatsApp did for messaging - here's what the BBC's technology editor found when she used it.
articles.body:
I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

How well Muse works really matters to Meta.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.

I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch.

"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," it says in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.

It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda - my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

articles.title: Bringing hostages home: How Trump revived Rome's citizen-first ethos
articles.summary: Like the Roman Empire retrieving its citizens, President Donald Trump has freed every Gaza hostage and over 100 detained Americans.
articles.body: "Today America is the Roman Empire and New York is Rome itself." — John Lennon When Rome lost a citizen to a foreign power, it did not negotiate from a position of weakness or wait for the right diplomatic moment to engage. It sent legions. Its actions were swift and total because Rome understood what no one else did: that a citizen is not a statistic, but the living proof that the state exists to protect its own. To be a Roman citizen was to carry the full weight of the Republic on your back. That protection wasn’t a privilege you earned or a favor you begged for; it was your right, simply for being Roman. And when that right was violated, the Republic didn’t file a complaint or turn a blind eye; it came to get you. ADVOCATE REVEALS FREED MARINE VET'S PHYSICAL, MENTAL TORMENT IN RUSSIAN PRISON AS 5 AMERICANS REMAIN HELD The young Julius Caesar learned this early. Captured by Cilician pirates in 75 B.C., he spent 38 days in their hands, joking that they had no idea who they had taken. When his ransom arrived, and he was freed, he raised a fleet, hunted them down and crucified every last one of them. That was Rome. You do not take a Roman and live to tell about it. That is the standard and the ethos that President Donald Trump has restored to America. Under President Trump’s steadfast leadership, this administration has brought home a record-breaking more than 100 unjustly detained Americans, including securing the release of every last hostage in Gaza — living and deceased. But the numbers are not the story. The story is the principle underneath them. And that principle is what sets this administration apart from all the others and why it is so successful at bringing Americans home. It’s simple: This administration does not treat the rescue of Americans as a burden to be managed or a category to be triaged. It treats it as a sacred mission, rooted in an ancient Western ideal: the state exists to protect its people, and no one is left behind. TRUMP SAYS IRAN RELEASED AMERICAN WOMAN HELD SINCE 2024 IN 'GESTURE OF GOODWILL' As in the Roman Republic, American citizens are the core of this nation — and abandoning one is a stain on the whole. This instinct is clearly visible in the personal promises President Trump has made and kept, like the one made to Marc Fogel’s 95-year-old mother, and in his willingness to use hard leverage against Venezuela, Russia, the Taliban and Hamas. Moreover, under President Trump, that ethos is backed by an executive order that lets the State Department designate countries as state sponsors of wrongful detention and hit them with meaningful sanctions. The sheer credibility of President Trump’s policy of "peace through strength," which makes adversaries calculate that holding an American costs more than releasing one, combined with the personal dealmaking style that builds direct relationships with strongmen instead of relying on slow multilateral channels, is another reason this administration succeeds where others have failed. Moreover, the president’s explicit elevation of the issue to a top priority means that every embassy and envoy knows this is what the president measures himself by — and expects from them. That bias for action is the operational engine behind the historic numbers. Hostage negotiations usually die in process — committees, risk assessments, endless interagency reviews — while the clock runs on the person in the cell. This administration treats speed as a moral duty, not a risk. The contrast is sharp. The Biden administration let cases drag on for years — like the slow, bureaucratic approach that left people like Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan in limbo while lawyers and diplomats traded notes and held endless meetings. As in the Roman Republic, American citizens are the core of this nation — and abandoning one is a stain on the whole. President Trump’s team moves with purpose and alacrity in days or weeks, not years, because they see delay as a form of abandonment. And that includes all elements of the president’s team, from across the U.S. government, including the Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs, the FBI’s Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell, the National Security Council’s counterterrorism directorate and Special Presidential Envoy for Peace Steve Witkoff. US MARINE VETERAN RELEASED FROM RUSSIAN PRISON AFTER 1,666 DAYS OF DETENTION Previous administrations waited for the other side to offer a deal, then spent months studying it. The Trump administration seizes openings the moment they appear or, better yet, creates them. When a window cracks open — a diplomatic thaw, a backchannel, a shift in a foreign leader’s incentives — they move through it before it closes, and if a case stalls, pressure is increased to create opportunity. That opportunism and decisiveness are what turned a stalled Gaza process into a completed deal and brought former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman home from Russia, as well as Joseph St. Clair and 23 other Americans home from Venezuela. Whereas Biden’s team treated these cases as liabilities — something to manage, contain and quietly resolve without drawing attention — the Trump administration inverts that entirely. There’s no triage here. No ranking cases by profile or political cost. No telling families to go away or be quiet. President Trump’s team tackles every case head-on, offering full transparency and accountability, because every American is a citizen of the republic, and the republic owes them all — just ask the families who have unfettered access to the entire hostage enterprise, including White House officials, from day one. Our refusal to categorize is what makes the mission sacred and righteous, rather than bureaucratic. Our team stays with the person — rehab, counseling, rebuilding a life that captivity tried to erase. And when justice demands it, we go after the perpetrators themselves. The message is unmistakable: Take an American, and you will pay. Not someday, not maybe. You will regret it. That’s the Roman part in full. Rome didn’t just retrieve its citizens; it made the cost of taking one so high that few dared try again. The republic protected its own, and it punished those who harmed them. The Trump administration carries that same standard and is united under that same coda because to be an American is something unique and special, envied by the world over and worth preserving: Every American home, every American family whole and every enemy who thought they could profit from Americans’ suffering left to count the price and the bodies.

articles.summary: Donald Trump flirts with Medicare for All as Abdul El-Sayed pitches "Trumpcare," though an NBC survey found 82% of Americans like their coverage.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is hinting that he might find common ground with incoming Democrats who are promising "affordability." In particular, he has signaled a willingness to work with Massachusetts Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren on capping credit card interest rates and perhaps even with Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on promoting universal healthcare. These are terrible ideas. The president will not rebuild his popularity or dampen Democrats’ impeachment zeal by climbing aboard failed notions that will hurt the economy. Indeed, just the opposite is true. Trump should accept that the zealots eager to impeach him and punish his associates will not give up. Democrats know they were not elected because American voters have suddenly lost their enthusiasm for free enterprise. Instead, surveys have shown that Trump was indeed on the midterm ballot and was rejected by MAGA and Democrats alike. TRUMP SAYS HE 'CAN'T IMAGINE' DEMOCRATS WILL IMPEACH HIM A THIRD TIME Moderate Democrats and even some on the left are warning that endless impeachments and investigations could hurt Democrats. Former Democratic New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio cautioned exactly that recently on a "Cats Roundtable" on 770 WABC. While acknowledging "there will be some investigations of one thing or another," he urged his party to not "get lost in that stuff. People don’t want bickering and endless negativity." He’s right, but the tail wagging the dog of the Democratic Party may not care. The furious left threatens to primary established Democrats across the country as we approach 2028. While the liberal media keeps reassuring us that it is "moderate Democrats" who are now taking over Washington, it is clear that even supposed centrists like incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries cannot resist the siren call of survival. JAMIE RASKIN CALLS CONCERNS OVER SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP A MEDIA 'NARRATIVE' As to teaming up with Warren to cap interest rates, specifically holding rates at 10%, Trump is playing with fire. Speaking with Kayleigh McEnany on Fox News over the weekend, Trump suggested he was open to a one-year cap on interest rates and fees charged by lenders. He told the former White House press secretary, "I would do it," adding, "These credit card companies have made a lot and the credit card fees that they charge, I'm all into it." The president acknowledged, "I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise, but what's free enterprise when you're sitting home, and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue, and they said, 'Let's charge a fee that's too high,'" he continued. "So, I'm all for that." This is not a new idea for Trump, who first suggested capping credit card rates during the 2024 presidential campaign. The problem with putting an artificial lid on interest rates, even if it’s for a limited time, is that credit card companies will respond by restricting credit. The reason rates are as high as they are, with some companies charging more than 20% interest, is that those lenders are facing high costs, and for some, have to charge more to compensate for losses. If you mandate lower rates, it will be the high-risk or subprime borrower who immediately loses access to credit. An analysis from the Committee to Unleash Prosperity, drawing on a survey of credit markets published by the American Bankers Association (an interested party, to be sure), concluded that 74% to 85% of existing credit card accounts could be closed or have credit lines reduced, affecting between 137 million and 159 million cardholders. This is pretty fundamental and quite drastic. Opposition to a cap is also backed by research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York examining usury limits, which are legal caps on the interest rates that lenders can charge. The study finds that these caps, imposed by various states, lead to reduced lending to riskier borrowers. MEDICARE FOR ALL SOUNDS FREE. BUT WAIT UNTIL YOU SEE YOUR HUGE TAX BILL Consumer debt has increased. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reports that nationwide credit card balances have risen 67% since the beginning of 2021, helping to drive consumer spending. Pull the rug out from borrowers, and the economy will sink like a stone. As to teaming up with Warren to cap interest rates, specifically holding rates at 10%, Trump is playing with fire. As to possibly joining newly elected El-Sayed’s push for Medicare for All, Trump is going where no sane president should venture. El-Sayed is cleverly courting the president, flattering him by calling his proposal "Trumpcare," and posting a photo of a gold credit card, which the president reposted. Trump must resist. DEPROGRAMMED: A 'KIND OFFER' OF DEATH SENT THIS COUPLE RUNNING FROM UNIVERSAL HEALTH CARE The horrors of government-run healthcare in the U.K. and in Canada are well known. Lengthy wait times and rationed healthcare are pervasive in those countries, as is unhappiness with their systems. In 2025, only "26% of British adults were satisfied with how the NHS runs," according to a British Social Attitudes survey which has been conducted yearly since 1983 by the National Centre for Social Research. The 2025 tally was considered a victory as it was up from an all-time low of 21% in 2024. HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' Compare that to an NBC survey last year which found a resounding 82% of Americans satisfied with their health insurance coverage, including most older Americans and those on Medicare and Medicaid. Only 18% were unhappy with their coverage. About two-thirds of Americans have private health insurance, the majority provided by their employer. Under earlier proposals embraced by El-Sayed and Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, private insurance would no longer be available. Progressives have tempered those suggestions of late, aware that the majority of the country will not stand to have their reliable program snatched away. THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS This is especially true for union households, which enjoy the luxury of Cadillac health benefits negotiated on their behalf. With Democrats struggling to hold onto blue-collar voters, undermining union wins would not be welcome. articles.title: Israeli air strikes in Gaza kill 7 as doctors warn of meningitis outbreak
articles.summary: Gaza health officials say meningitis cases rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the typical monthly rate.
articles.body:
At least seven Palestinians, including a child and police officers, have been killed and dozens injured in Israeli air strikes on the Gaza Strip.

Health officials confirmed the deaths on Tuesday morning while a public health warning was issued about an outbreak of meningitis.

Three Palestinians, including a child, were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Wadi Gaza area in the centre of the Strip, medical sources said.

Earlier on Tuesday morning, a further three Palestinians were killed and five wounded when an Israeli drone struck the al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza while a fourth Palestinian died from injuries after being targeted in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary reported from Gaza that the three people killed in the al-Mawasi attack were Palestinian police officers. “Dozens of others have been injured in different areas across the Gaza Strip,” she said on Tuesday. “According to the Ministry of Health, it was very hard to recognise who these people were who were attacked by Israeli forces, and the same thing happened yesterday when Israeli forces targeted a vehicle in Gaza City.”

“There have been attacks on a daily basis by Israeli forces despite the fact that there has been a ‘ceasefire’ that has been agreed on between both parties,” Khoudary said. “Israel continues to violate this ‘ceasefire’ every single day.”

On Monday night, two civilians were also killed and others injured in an air strike by Israeli forces on Gaza City, Wafa reported.

The Ministry of Health in the Gaza Strip has also issued an epidemic alert across all parts of Gaza due to a rapid rise in cases of meningitis. It warned that the spread of the disease poses a direct threat to the lives of thousands of Palestinians, particularly children, given the deteriorating health and environmental conditions in the Strip.

Dr Nidal Ghoneim, deputy director general of primary care for public health affairs, said at a news conference that cases of meningitis rose to 272 in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate, which ranges from 30 to 50 cases.

Ghoneim explained that 15 deaths resulting from the disease have been recorded since the start of this year, including five deaths in August, September and October. He noted a rise in cases of bacterial meningitis, which is the most serious form of the illness, from 10 to 20 cases per month to 108 cases in October. Since the start of November, another 100 cases have been recorded, he said.

According to health officials, casualties from Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza have risen to 74,746 people killed and 176,234 injured since it began on October 7, 2023. That includes 1,679 people killed and 6,100 injured since the “ceasefire” went into effect on October 10 last year.

articles.title: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times
articles.summary: Published extracts from the late pontiff's diary claim one of the visions happened "in the choir loft" during Mass.
articles.body:
Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.

In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.

"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.

In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.

Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign .

"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.

"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."

Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.

"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.

He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.

"I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".

The late pope also revealed that while getting ready to go to sleep in June 2018, he "saw the gates of hell".

"I watched a little, and it terrified me," he said, adding that he "took the rosary as a weapon".

"It's dangerous to get close to the gates of hell, because flames can spring out and burn," he wrote.

Cardinal Victor Fernandez, head of the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and friend of Francis, edited the diaries, which are the first by a pope to be released to the public since the 1960s.

Pope Francis was elected pope in 2013 and died aged 88 in April 2025.

articles.title: Iraq orders takeover of oilfields in areas under Kurdish control
articles.summary: PM Ali al-Zaidi also orders his government to seize all crossings in the Kurdish region after an oil smuggling inquiry.
articles.body:
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous region in the north of the country.

The prime minister’s order covers oilfields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces, according to a statement from his office on Tuesday.

It said Baghdad would “secure and monitor all oilfields with cameras, including fields within the administrative boundaries of the federal government that are under the security authority of the regional government”.

Al-Zaidi also ordered the border crossings authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdish region and directed the regional government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal Oil Ministry.

“The Border Forces Command shall close unofficial crossings along the international borders with neighbouring countries, including crossings in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq,” the statement said, adding that “all seasonal roads” between the four governorates and the Kurdish region would be closed.

Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Baghdad, said the latest development might exacerbate tensions and disputes over control of oil and the sharing of budgetary resources between the national government and the autonomous regional government.

“The federal government is keen to keep all excavation and marketing of oil under its state organisation, SOMO, but this has been totally rejected by the Kurdish region,” he said.

A dispute over Kurdish authorities selling oil without Baghdad’s approval halted pipeline shipments to Turkiye for more than two years before the sides agreed in September 2025 to restart them.

Al-Zaidi, meanwhile, removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company’s director general and his deputies pending further investigation, Iraq’s state news agency reported.

In a separate case, Iraqi officials accused Kataib Hezbollah, an armed group backed by Iran, of running an oil smuggling network in its stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad.

articles.title: Down the Rabbit Hole: Decoding the GTA VI craze for normies and non-gamers
articles.summary: In British politics in the early noughties, it was said that the most terrifying words in the political lexicon were: “Michael Crick is in reception.” The
articles.body: In British politics in the early noughties, it was said that the most terrifying words in the political lexicon were: “Michael Crick is in reception.” The words reflected the sheer terror generated in British political circles by the “terrier-like reputation” of Crick, whose journalism, combining unstinting principles with inexhaustible research, made even the most seasoned politicians, used to the most putrid tabloids, quake in their boots.But the times change, and those who don’t change with the times are often the subject of some ridicule, as Crick learned when he tweeted his outrage about GTA VI on the BBC, calling it a “ridiculous puff (piece)” and “appalling free advertising”.Crick’s diatribe led Piers Morgan, a man who moves with the alacrity of a bloodhound pouncing upon any outrage, to rebut him with “Calm down, Grandpa”.Now we live in a hyperconnected world, where we face being labelled outcasts, where one can be mocked for not weighing in on the ending of Game of Thrones, being excited about Avengers: Doomsday, or explaining why the first few soporific episodes of Breaking Bad are worth the wait.But even by those exalted standards, GTA VI seems to have become a hitherto unseen cultural phenomenon that has consumed everything in its wake.The blurb of JRR Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings used to read: “The English-speaking world is divided into those who have read Lord of the Rings, and those who are going to read Lord of the Rings.” The same applies to GTA VI: even if not everyone plays the game, everyone will be part of the conversation.Now, if, like Crick, you are scratching your head about how a video game with a grammatically wonky (but legally sound) title became a global phenomenon, here’s a primer.GTA VI for NoobsThere was a time when gamers were often chided by their mothers for wasting time on video games. Today, it’s usually their wives doing the chiding, but it’s kind of ironic given that Nvidia’s chips, from a company that cut its teeth by making GPUs for gaming nerds, are the foundation upon which the modern AI frontier model race is built.To understand the GTA phenomenon, we have to take a small walk through the history of video games, which, in popular imagination, started with two white rectangles hitting a white dot across a black screen. That might sound like an exaggeration, but that’s one of the earliest commercially successful video games, called Pong, released by Atari in 1972. The graphics became better with time, with a dot becoming a spaceship in Space Invaders (1978) and a yellow circle in Pac-Man (1980). Then came the gaming console era, where aeons were wasted getting an Italian plumber or a parkour-loving prince to rescue a pixelated princess.Soon, gaming moved from addictive pixels in a 2D world to a more open space.At this time, a company in Scotland named DMA Design, founded by David Jones, developed a game called Race ‘n’ Chase that involved police officers pursuing criminals. That turned out to be inordinately, mind-numbingly boring, so the company flipped the script and made the criminal the protagonist, and Grand Theft Auto was first released in 1997.And thus we got the most famous Scottish export since whisky and Sean Connery, with each open world based on a real city. The game arrived at a time when politicians discovered that, rather than take responsibility, video games, along with rock music, comic books and television, could be blamed for the moral degradation of society. They were certainly helped by notorious British publicist Max Clifford, who understood that the easiest way to sell something was to get elected officials to deride it. GTA was discussed in the House of Lords – which, given its antecedents, would be a perfect location for a GTA spinoff – and got the kind of publicity money cannot buy.Onscreen, the revolution happened when GTA went from a bird’s-eye, two-dimensional Flatland look to a full three-dimensional open world with GTA III, where one could do everything one wants to do in the real world but cannot because one’s constitution is too delicate for jail: run over pedestrians, sell drugs and do other things that are frowned upon in civil society.The latest instalment, GTA VI, takes us back to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami in the state of Leonida, Rockstar’s take on Florida where all the folks are doing things that allows us to create the Florida man headlines.This time the protagonists are couple Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Jason is a former soldier and Lucia GTA’s first female protagonist which is enough to heckle incels across the world. And much like its predecessors, the actual storyline is only part of the attraction, since players are free to ignore it and spend their time doing whatever they please, provided the game's creators have programmed it.While explaining the much-debated New York Times 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century, the Times’ chief television critic James Poniewozik explained that The Sopranos didn’t make the cut because it premiered in 1999, but its legacy was writ large in the antihero dramas that made the cut, including its top three offerings: Breaking Bad, The Wire and Mad Men. The same goes for the GTA series, where we’ve overwhelmingly batted for the chance to roleplay as deeply problematic protagonists without having to pay for our sins, as Plato explored all those centuries ago in The Republic through the story of the Ring of Gyges, which would appear to be an inspiration for Gollum and the LOTR ring.One could even go further and say that the current state of the world, where the most powerful nation is led by a self-aggrandising leader who doesn’t even pretend to couch his avarice in terms of politesse, as was the norm in politics before, is beginning to resemble a live-action version of GTA.GTA VI in NumbersNow every qualitative assessment can come down to a quantitative measure, particularly when a video game gets the sort of attention normally reserved for a World Cup final, a general election result or the death of a monarch.The numbers make for remarkable reading.When GTA V was released in September 2013, it earned over $800 million in retail sales within 24 hours and crossed the billion-dollar mark in three days, making it the fastest entertainment product in history to reach that milestone.For context, Avengers: Endgame, which involved the combined efforts of nearly every superhero Marvel had managed to assemble over a decade, took five days to reach $1 billion at the box office.GTA VI, released on November 19, 2026, made those figures look like petty change.According to Rockstar Games, GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day, including pre-orders, with 32.5 million copies sold before release. GTA VI, meanwhile, had already sold a staggering 32.5 million copies before it was even released. GTA V sold 235 million copies since 2013, taking the total number of copies, including GTA VI pre-sales, to approximately 512 million.YouTube states that content related to the GTA franchise has accumulated 900 billion views on the platform, while GTA VI-related videos attracted 40 billion views before the game hit the shelves.The release itself attracted 7.91 million concurrent viewers across livestreaming platforms, with gamers collectively watching more than 125 million hours of GTA VI streams in the first 24 hours.But perhaps the most astonishing number is 13.13 years separated GTA V and GTA VI. When the former was released, Barack Obama was US president, Narendra Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat, Manchester United were serial Premier League winners, and the idea of a former reality star upending the world order was laughable.But perhaps the metric that shows GTA’s stickiness is the fact that between 2013 and 2025, GTA V remained among YouTube’s ten most-viewed games every single year. In a world where it’s almost impossible to remember what happened between two seasons – and can anyone really tell the Targaryen siblings apart in House of the Dragon? – GTA maintained its cultural relevance.The Cultural Impact of GTA VIEven before GTA VI dropped, the cultural impact of the game became evident. The moment the first trailer came out, featuring Tom Petty’s 1989 song Love Is a Long Road, the song saw a 36,979% surge in Spotify streams, eventually crossing 40 million streams. The first trailer on YouTube racked up 93 million views in 24 hours and a total of over 310 million views.In India, which has an estimated 550 million gamers, mostly on mobile games, GTA VI was released on the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, making it inaccessible to anyone who didn’t own a compatible console or have access to one. Yet, on the day of its release, gaming cafés across the country were jam-packed, with many taking leave from work to play.Like all things on the internet, it also immediately became a cultural flashpoint, with many complaining that GTA VI was too sanitised because it forces the protagonist to fix sinks, go on dates and even work out, things that people log in to their video games to avoid doing in the real world.Influential streamer Asmongold complained about having to repair a sink, rub Lucia's feet and listen to her friends' stories, while others complained that the game had become too 'woke'. A game that was once deemed to be responsible for moral degradation in the real world was now being accused of replicating it too exactly.The game's most enduring contribution to internet culture, however, might be the meme “We got this before GTA VI”, which became a shorthand for events that nobody thought would happen before the game was released.In the thirteen years between GTA V and GTA VI, we witnessed a global pandemic, the death of Queen Elizabeth II, Messi winning the World Cup, Donald Trump winning the White House twice, and the rise of generative AI, which means that humanity managed to create machines capable of writing poetry, generating videos and replacing white-collar workers before Rockstar managed to release another GTA. The meme became so popular that when GTA VI finally arrived, internet users started mourning its demise, while some pointed out that we had even got the end of the “We got this before GTA VI” meme before GTA VI.Brands, governments and even military alliances decided to jump on the bandwagon. Singapore wondered why folks couldn’t remember the MRT map. Miami police reminded gamers that, unlike the game, their city had rules. KFC had a mock funeral for “Ann Alibi”. The White House released a GTA-inspired video while PM Narendra Modi used GTA V vs GTA VI to highlight the Centre’s developmental work.Twenty-nine years after politicians worried about the moral degradation caused by a fictional world, that world’s cultural baggage had become too much for the real world to ignore. One wonders what Max Clifford, who understood the value of manufacturing outrage, would have made of a world where prime ministers, presidents and military alliances were doing Rockstar’s publicity for free.As Bob Dylan warned in The Times They Are A-Changin’: “Your sons and your daughters are beyond your command.” Six decades later, the parents and politicians seem to have finally got the message.Now it’s their turn to sing the children’s tune.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Nurses in Northern Ireland vote for industrial action over pay
articles.summary: Nurses will take continuous action short of strike from 3 December - such action includes working to rule and a ban on overtime.
articles.body:
Nurses in Northern Ireland have voted overwhelmingly to take industrial action, including strike action, over pay.

They will take continuous action short of strike from 3 December - this sort of action includes working to rule and a ban on overtime.

The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) said it was working with other unions for a collective day of strike action, which one its leaders said would probably be early January.

The RCN said the industrial action was the result of the failure of the Northern Ireland Executive and Department of Health to implement the 2026-27 pay award.

A pay review body recommended a 3.3% rise for Agenda for Change staff, which includes nurses, health visitors, midwives, ambulance staff, porters and cleaners, from April this year.

While nursing staff in England and Wales have received their pay awards, nurses in Northern Ireland are still waiting for theirs.

RCN members working in health and social care can now be expected on the picket lines again, seven years after voting yes to taking strike action for the first time in Northern Ireland .

The union said 93% of its members who responded , voted to take action short of strike and strike action.

Prof Rita Devlin, executive director of the RCN in Northern Ireland, said the result sent "an unequivocal message" to the Northern Ireland Executive and the Department of Health that nursing staff would "no longer tolerate this annual cycle of uncertainty, delay and disregard when it comes to their pay".

She said nursing staff in Northern Ireland were being left behind "because of a failure to provide the necessary funding".

Devlin said members were "being forced into industrial action" to secure the pay award they are due, rather than being focused solely on delivering patient care.

"Nursing staff do not take the decision to strike lightly," she said.

"They understand better than anyone the challenges facing our health service and the impact industrial action can have.

"But they have reached a point where they feel they have no other option."

As winter pressure are building across the health and social care system, Devlin said the last place nurses want to be is on a picket line.

"Responsibility for this situation sits squarely with our political leaders, who have once again failed to ensure nursing staff are treated fairly and paid on time," she added.

articles.title: China walks ‘thin line’ in push to prevent another Horn of Africa war
articles.summary: Beijing has escalated diplomatic efforts to ease tensions involving Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti.
articles.body:
Beijing, China – China has stepped up diplomatic efforts in the Horn of Africa, sending senior envoys to four countries to ease mounting tensions that threaten to plunge the region into another devastating conflict.

Beijing’s special representative for African affairs, Liu Xianfa, travelled to Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt in early November, while its special envoy for Horn of Africa affairs, Hu Changchun, visited Eritrea. They met senior officials, including Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and the foreign ministers of Ethiopia and Egypt.

Announcing the visits on November 2, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said they were aimed at “promoting talks for peace, easing tensions, and playing a constructive role for upholding regional peace and stability”.

The visits followed a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, raising fears of another war between the neighbours. Meanwhile, longstanding disputes involving Egypt threaten to draw other countries into a wider confrontation.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a devastating border war between 1998 and 2000, killing tens of thousands of people. A historic peace agreement in 2018 ended two decades of hostility, but their reconciliation began to unravel following Ethiopia’s civil war in the northern Tigray region.

Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian government troops against Tigrayan fighters, but Eritrea was excluded from the 2022 peace agreement that ended the main phase of the war.

Central to their latest dispute is Ethiopia’s push to secure access to the Red Sea. The country has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993 and relies heavily on neighbouring Djibouti’s ports for international trade. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed argues access to the sea is essential for his country’s future, but his government’s interest in Eritrea’s strategic port of Assab has raised fears in Asmara over its territorial sovereignty.

Both governments accuse each other of supporting armed groups.

Complicating matters is Ethiopia’s longstanding dispute with Egypt over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile. Cairo fears the project could threaten its water supply, while Addis Ababa insists it has the right to harness the river for electricity generation and economic development.

Egypt has strengthened its relationship with Eritrea, adding another dimension to the growing tensions. Recent reports of Ethiopian and Eritrean troops gathering near their shared border have heightened fears of a wider conflict.

China has billions of dollars at stake in the Horn of Africa, which sits along one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes. Between 2000 and 2023, China committed $17.8bn in loans to Ethiopia, according to United States-based research institute AidData.

Edson Ziso, a visiting research fellow at the University of Adelaide, says China has played a “starring role” in Ethiopia’s economic transformation. Among Beijing’s flagship infrastructure projects is the $4.3bn Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, which connects landlocked Ethiopia to the coast.

Meanwhile, Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military base, which opened in 2017. The country sits near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a crucial shipping passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. “The Strait of Hormuz stalemate has already highlighted the huge cost conflict can inflict on the global economy when vital shipping lanes are choked,” says Ziso.

China’s efforts also reflect President Xi Jinping’s desire to portray his country as a major diplomatic player and contributor to global peace and stability, say analysts. Beijing has promoted what it calls the “Outlook on Peace and Development in the Horn of Africa”, a 2022 framework that emphasises African-led solutions to security challenges.

Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow with the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, says Beijing’s approach is focused on helping countries in the region “control their security destiny”, rather than imposing solutions from outside. She says Beijing’s view is that “development gaps fuel instability,” but success depends on all parties accepting that “confrontation leaves all of them worse off.”

China’s close relationships with governments across the region put it in a position to encourage dialogue, but its ability to broker meaningful compromises remains unclear.

Beijing’s principle of noninterference has helped it cultivate relationships across Africa. Yet the disputes involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt concern deeply sensitive questions of territory, sovereignty and water security. Economic incentives may not be enough to resolve them, caution analysts.

Among the obstacles, Khan says, are actors outside the region who have “stoked confrontation and disrupted African-led processes”. Ziso says the involvement of proxy forces, fighter groups and rebels also presents a significant challenge.

And while all regional countries have close ties with Beijing, some, particularly Egypt, have longstanding security relationships with Washington. Ziso says this could limit China’s ability to achieve a breakthrough if governments perceive Chinese-led solutions as jeopardising relations with the US.

Against that backdrop, China’s recent diplomatic visits have produced statements of support for greater cooperation and regional peace, but no formal negotiations or concrete agreements have been announced.

“China is thus walking a thin line,” Ziso says, adding that all four countries – Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti – are critical to Beijing’s economic and strategic interests. “China may need to look beyond its own interests in pursuit of concrete and sustainable de-escalation.”

articles.title: Baby Peter's mother Tracey Connelly given open prison recommendation
articles.summary: Tracey Connelly was first sentenced in 2009 over the death of her toddler son Peter.
articles.body:
The mother of the toddler known as Baby P - who died after months of abuse - has been told she will not be freed from jail, although the Parole Board has recommended she should be moved to an open prison.

Tracey Connelly, now 45, was jailed in 2009 for causing or allowing the death of her 17-month-old son Peter at their home in Tottenham, north London, in August 2007.

Connelly has been freed twice, in October 2013 and July 2022, and recalled to prison both times, in February 2015 and August 2024.

Public parole hearings took place last October, but the case was adjourned after the panel decided there needed to be a further psychological assessment.

Peter suffered more than 50 injuries, despite being on the at-risk register and receiving 60 visits from social workers, police officers and health professionals over eight months.

Connelly's then-boyfriend Steven Barker and his brother, Jason Owen, were also convicted of causing or allowing the death of 17-month-old Peter.

Giving evidence to the Parole Board review, which was livestreamed from prison, Connelly admitted she had been a "horrendous" mother who "knew deep down" that Barker was abusing her son, but she had wanted her Prince Charming and her children "paid for that".

She said she never intended to live with anyone again or be around other people's children. "I want to be the CEO of my own home and my own life," she told the review.

'I was a bad parent', Baby P's mother tells panel

At the Old Bailey in 2009, Connelly was given an indeterminate sentence for public protection (IPP), which allowed prisoners to be held beyond their minimum term and kept on licence for years after release.

Such sentences were abolished in 2012, and recent reforms mean licences now end after a set period without recall. The panel said that but for these reforms it would have released her again on strict licence conditions.

The Parole Board said that "somewhat ironically" a measure meant to address the unfairness of IPP sentences had made it harder to free Connelly.

Every professional who gave evidence supported her release, but lawyers for the Justice Secretary Alex Norris opposed it, citing Connelly's history of deception, her failure to disclose relationships and an assessment rating her a high risk of serious harm to children.

A spokesperson for the Parole Board said: "This was a recommendation only and the secretary of state for justice considers the advice before making the final decision on whether a prisoner is suitable for open conditions.

"We will only make a recommendation for open conditions if a Parole Board panel is satisfied that the risk to the public has reduced sufficiently to be manageable in an open prison."

articles.title: ‘We’ll keep sinking Russian ships’: Ukraine challenges Putin’s global reach
articles.summary: Ukraine’s strike off Libya signals Kyiv’s ability to challenge Russian influence beyond the front lines.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – The Merkury warship was one of the newest Russian warships equipped with antiship, surface-to-air and cruise missiles and an advanced three-dimensional radar.

The corvette, commissioned three years ago, escorted the Western-sanctioned Angara freighter that was transporting weapons and military equipment to the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi as part of Russia’s “Libyan Express” route, according to Ukrainian intelligence.

Seven Ukrainian-made naval drones launched from a mothership struck the Merkury and MV Angara on Sunday, Kyiv said. Ukraine claimed the corvette was sunk, while Libyan military officials told The Associated Press news agency that it was severely damaged.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike, 2,400km (1,500 miles) from the front lines of Ukraine, “exemplary”.

The operation was not, however, just about destroying another Russian warship. It was also intended to demonstrate Ukraine’s ability to strike at Moscow’s naval assets far beyond the Black Sea, undermining Russia’s efforts to project military power internationally.

The Sunday strike is “so far, a political demonstration from Ukraine of ‘we can do it,'” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevich told Al Jazeera.

“But if the attacks continue, Russia will find it more difficult to sell itself as a strong player.”

Tyshkevich said the attack could undermine Russia’s image as a powerful international ally, particularly among African governments and military authorities that have developed ties with Moscow.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have destroyed or damaged numerous Russian naval vessels.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli has condemned the attack.

The Kremlin uses assets in Benghazi, controlled by the eastern-based rival administration led by military renegade and leader of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) Khalifa Haftar, as a gateway to the Mediterranean, according to observers.

Russia has deployed radar and advanced air-defence systems to military facilities in Libya, strengthening its surveillance and military capabilities in the central Mediterranean, close to NATO’s southern flank.

Eastern Libya is a maritime entry and logistics hub for Russia’s military presence in North Africa and the Sahel. While Moscow uses military transport aircraft to move personnel and lighter cargo, heavy equipment and supplies are also transported by sea.

Ports, particularly Tobruk and Benghazi, provide access for Russian cargo vessels, with facilities for docking, unloading and resupply. Eastern Libya also connects Mediterranean maritime routes with inland military airbases, including al-Khadim and al-Jufra, and southern transport corridors leading towards the Sahara and the Sahel, where Russia maintains military deployments.

The strike offers a perfect formula to further interrupt Russia’s Sahel operations, said a drone maker in Ukraine.

“This is the way. We’ll keep sinking [Russian ships] one by one. Easy does it,” Andrey Pronin, a pioneer of drone warfare, told Al Jazeera.

The amount of damage is not clear yet, but Russia has promised revenge .

“Even in Moscow, they don’t understand the scale of the damage; it will have to be assessed,” Ruslan Suleymanov, an associate fellow at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a United States-British think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Eastern Libyan areas controlled by Haftar – and Benghazi in particular – have become “a key hub from the logistical viewpoint” for the Russian military in the Middle East and North Africa since the 2024 fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, Suleymanov said.

The Sunday attack is “a heavy blow, in terms of [Moscow’s international] image too; it shows at least that the war is going on not just in Ukraine, but also on other fronts, and that of course, the Russian military is very vulnerable, including in the Libyan areas”, he said.

For years, Russia has been expanding its footprint in the Sahel, offering military support and economic cooperation to Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso.

Ukraine said the Angara was carrying Russian military equipment as part of Moscow’s military supply network in Libya, which supports its wider military presence in Africa, including the Sahel.

At least partially, Ukraine “destroyed the sea component of the African Corps supply”, Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s Bremen University, told Al Jazeera, referring to the Kremlin-backed military force operating in Africa.

Guided by the “my-enemy’s-enemy-is-my-friend” principle, Kyiv has been trying to aid anti-Moscow forces despite their affiliations.

Syrian rebels who overthrew al-Assad in 2024 received drones and other military supplies from Ukraine, The Washington Post reported.

Kyiv sent about 20 drone operators and some 150 drones to help the Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) opposition group based in Idlib, the paper claimed, citing sources familiar with Ukrainian military operations abroad.

Ukrainian special forces helped Syrian rebels “destroy” Russian mercenaries in southern Syria, the Kyiv Post reported in June 2024.

“Russia as a global player faces the rising influence of Ukraine as a global player – and it happens in the regions where it doesn’t expect to face it,” Mitrokhin said.

He doubts, however, the practicality of hitting Russia wherever it hurts – and suspects the Pentagon’s involvement in strikes against Moscow.

“What I see in it is Zelenskyy striving to prove to Putin that Ukraine can ‘compete with Russia globally’ or at least in hotspots,” he said.

“I don’t rule out that Ukraine causes trouble to Russia at the request or with maximal support from the US military, that tries to limit Russia’s growing clout in these areas without getting their own hands dirty and without a direct conflict with Russia,” he said.

The Sunday operation may complicate efforts by the Malian military and Russia’s Africa Corps to consolidate their positions in northern Mali, Mitrokhin said.

At least 15 Ukrainian drone pilots help the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) fight Mali’s military government despite their links to the Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin group affiliated with al-Qaeda, CNN reported in September.

CNN cited a Ukrainian defence intelligence source as saying Ukrainian drone experts were also stationed in Sudan and trained troops from Chad, Niger and Burkina Faso in Mali.

Ukraine’s use of minimal resources to help Russia’s enemies contrasts with NATO’s slowness and indecisiveness.

“While the alliance’s nations act indecisively, and Putin sees it as a weakness and ups the escalation, Ukraine finds a way to fight the enemy in a very complicated situation,” Lieutenant General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s General Staff of Armed Forces, told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: China probes Shanghai party boss, Politburo’s Chen Jining
articles.summary: Shanghai’s party chief Chen Jining, a member of China’s elite Politburo, is under investigation, the state-run Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since 2025.
articles.body: Shanghai’s party chief Chen Jining, a member of China’s elite Politburo, is under investigation, the state-run Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since 2025. China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” Xinhua said. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption. Before the unexpected announcement of the Chen probe, three Politburo members from the 24-member body formed in 2022 — He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui — had already been purged. The investigation of Chen marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command. For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall. Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua University to become its president. He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub. The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles. Xi, China’s current leader, briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the Politburo’s Standing Committee, the country’s highest decision-making body. China’s second-ranking official, Premier Li Qiang, as well as Vice President Han Zheng, also held the Shanghai post before moving into central leadership roles.

articles.title: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home
articles.summary: The break-in took place at the family's country retreat in Norfolk, on the Sandringham Estate.
articles.body:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home on the Sandringham estate, police say.

Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall.

Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody.

The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters.

William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays.

Anmer Hall, a country retreat with 10 bedrooms, was a gift to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II following their wedding in 2011.

The red brick Georgian mansion is on the private Sandringham estate in Norfolk and is about two miles (3km) east from Sandringham House, one of the King's private residences.

The Prince and Princess's main home is on the Windsor Castle estate in Berkshire.

The Sandringham estate spans approximately 31 sq miles (80 sq km).

Members of the public can visit it, although Sandringham House and its gardens are currently closed.

The Royal Parkland, which is the woodland to the west of the main house, is open to the public all year round.

Many other members of the Royal Family also live on the estate, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved onto Marsh Farm in February.

articles.title: Hormuz oil traffic is down 40 percent: Are Iran’s tanker attacks working?
articles.summary: Attacks on tankers have increased, impacting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Iran has reiterated that it will use “ all available means ” to confront the United States naval blockade, as it has stepped up attacks on tankers attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, signalling potential escalation.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that they would “definitely not tolerate” the naval blockade, and would use “all our tools to confront this US aggression”.

“Iran has the right to use any available tool to defend itself in this regard,” he said.

The naval blockade has largely halted Iranian oil exports. It was first imposed in April, but was lifted following the June memorandum of understanding. The blockade was reinstated weeks later after the agreement collapsed.

As Iran’s economy is increasingly squeezed by the US-led economic sanctions, attacks on tankers have also gone up, affecting the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption to the flow of oil has triggered a global energy crisis.

What do we know about the attacks on tankers, and how frequent are they?

Attacks on oil tankers and commercial vessels have continued throughout the war, but more recently, a rising number of tankers have erupted in flames after hitting naval mines purportedly placed by Iran. More than 25 tankers have been hit in the past week alone.

According to reports, tankers have continued to make the dangerous journey through the waterway without seeking Iran’s approval, often travelling in the dark and without navigation transponders to avoid alerting Iranian officials.

However, this clandestine approach has come with its own problems.

On Tuesday morning, Iran’s navy said two oil tankers had hit mines and caught fire in the waterway, according to a statement reported by Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

According to the statement, the tankers entered a restricted zone east of the strait after turning off their navigation and identification systems.

The statement reiterated that the strait would not be opened until Iran’s objectives and demands were met, including halting hostilities, lifting the blockade and waiving sanctions, adding that “owners of oil tankers are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait.”

At the same time, the commander of the Iranian army, Amir Hatami, called for tightening the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, stressing that Tehran needed to make conditions more difficult.

“We must tighten our control over the Strait of Hormuz, our management of it must be stronger, and conditions must become more difficult for the enemy,” Iranian television quoted Hatami as saying, during a speech to senior army commanders at the Command and Staff University.

The head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) navy, Ali Ozmaei, also warned vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz against using unapproved shipping routes.

“The Strait of Hormuz is not a place to test unauthorised routes and ignore maritime warnings,” Ozmaei said, according to the ISNA news agency.

Despite the attacks, oil prices have fallen, with Brent crude futures at $88.35 per barrel as supplies recover . At one point, oil prices went past $120 per barrel.

So far, according to the AIS ship-tracking platform, in the past 24 hours, 28 ships have crossed the strait: 12 into the Gulf and 16 out of it, carrying an estimated 4.18 million barrels of oil.

However, because it only collects data from vessels with transponders on, loopholes – including the no-signal bypass routes – mean it is not an accurate count of how many ships are crossing the strait.

Still, it is a huge drop from pre-war numbers, during which 125 to 140 ships used to pass through daily.

In the past week, Iran has also carried out attacks on US bases in the Gulf, targeting radars.

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Iran had launched “more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year”, adding that they had all been downed and had caused no damage.

Meanwhile, last week, US Central Command ( CENTCOM ) said in an advisory that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”, which had allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets.

But Iran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to hamper its trade.

According to data from Marine Traffic, a ship-tracking platform, the number of vessels crossing between November 1 and 23 has dropped as the month goes on.

In the first week of November, between the 1st and 7th, 226 vessels entered or exited the Gulf. In the last week of the month, from the 17th to the 23rd, only 125 vessels crossed the waterway. That’s a drop of more than 40 percent.

Throughout the month, the highest day with 29 vessels exiting took place on November 1, and the highest day entering the Gulf was November 7.

In contrast, the lowest day for exiting the Gulf was on Sunday, when only one vessel left the waterway; on the same day, only two vessels entered the waterway, the lowest figure for the month.
