articles.title: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return: Who are the big winners and losers?
articles.summary: Jensen Huang returns to lead the most consequential company powering the AI revolution. But who wins, who loses?
articles.body:
Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing face of the AI revolution, scandalously fell from the throne of the modern AI industry, he has reclaimed his leadership of the world’s most valuable semiconductor company, Nvidia .

It took a war room of Silicon Valley insiders lobbying the White House for US President Donald Trump to crack the whip on Monday and force chip giant Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang , 63, who fell from grace following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive and controlling shareholder of Megaspeed, an Nvidia client company that has since been blacklisted in the US.

What happens at Nvidia extends well beyond the California-based company.

Share values on the US stock market have become concentrated in a small group of increasingly valuable tech giants, which account for more than 60 percent of the Nasdaq-100. Tech and AI-linked companies together represent around half the S&P 500’s market value.

Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday triggered a 30 percent rise in Nvidia shares, but has raised several questions about the reach of the Trump administration’s dictates as investigations into the company and its CEO continue. It has also heightened worries about the future of AI development amid Washington’s deepening rivalry with Beijing.

We take a look at major winners and losers from this whole scandal.

The sacked CEO, who stunningly returned to applause from Nvidia employees on Monday, had left the board, which last week said it would not reinstate him.

From washing dishes at a Denny’s in the 1980s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang led Nvidia for nearly 33 years and became one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.

He now joins a number of “cult-style” leaders in Silicon Valley, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, who appear too “big” to fire.

Allegations that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, may have exposed restricted chip technology to Beijing were ultimately not enough to keep him out of the CEO’s office.

During the 11 days he was out of the office, media reports detailed at least two more extramarital affairs with employees at Nvidia, and revealed how he toxically berated his subordinates.

“If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again,” an Nvidia employee wrote on an internal platform, reported Wired.

Lloyd Blankfein, the former CEO of investment bank Goldman Sachs, wrote on X: “Guess you can come back from the graveyard if you’re really, really, really indispensable.”

For his part, President Trump argued that he just returned from a trip to China – where he attended the APEC summit and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping, “So I guess I’m involved also.”

Speaking with CNBC, Trump added, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” However, he said, “I don’t believe that’s true,” in the case of Huang. He did not comment on US intel reports he received.

The chip giant holds the key to the modern AI computing industry; its customers include Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, who rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.

Nvidia’s shares fell nearly 28 percent between November 11, when the board accepted Huang’s resignation, and November 20, amid mounting uncertainty over its future leadership.

By the end of Monday, November 23, Nvidia recovered approximately $956bn in market value, rising from its November 20 low of $3.04 trillion to $3.98 trillion, and remaining the world’s most valuable semiconductor company.

Among those shareholders is US President Trump. A review of Trump’s financial disclosures, first reported by The Washington Post, found that he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock at the end of August, up from about $1.3m at the end of 2024.

The AI industry at large felt the ripples from Huang’s exit from Nvidia, and his return is also boosting companies across the chip giant’s global supply chain, which are hoping for continuity in the product roadmap, manufacturing orders and investment plans.

Shares in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which manufactures Nvidia’s advanced AI processors, surged 9.9 percent on Tuesday, hitting the company’s daily trading limit and adding $158bn to its market value in a single session.

Shares in Foxconn, which assembles AI servers powered by Nvidia chips, also rose nearly 10 percent.

Shares in South Korean memory-chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics gained 6.7 percent and 6.6 percent, respectively.

Japanese chip-testing equipment maker Advantest shares jumped 12.5 percent.

On Tuesday, major Asian stock indexes in Seoul, Tokyo, and Taipei all rose.

Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against restrictions to tech exports, arguing that halting sales will surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.

That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.

The US first introduced export controls on the chips in 2022 and has subsequently tightened China’s access to them.

In one exception, following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping last year, Trump said he would allow H200 chip sales to approved Chinese customers. The US ‌eased ⁠its licensing policy for the powerful H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions.

Despite all the restrictions, Nvidia tech was reportedly still making its way to China, mostly via third countries and smuggling, according to media reports.

Since the Jensen Huang scandal came to light, Nvidia says it has stopped shipping powerful chips to China, but did not specify the reason for doing so.

President Trump, who backed Huang solidly, was quick to claim credit for the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang. But his administration has appeared divided over the issue.

The Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are continuing to investigate the company, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has emerged as one of its most vocal critics.

Bessent earlier questioned whether Nvidia had facilitated irregular chip sales to China to bolster its financial performance, alleging in an interview with Fox News that the AI chip giant had engaged in “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings”.

He has also called for Nvidia to appoint a new chief executive from outside the company.

Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces allegations that he delayed restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, raising questions about whether his decisions were influenced by the financial interests of his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now controlled by his two sons.

Nvidia’s board has 11 directors, including Huang.

After Huang resigned, board chair Harvey Jones told investors that he had left voluntarily and would not be reinstated, amid a mounting “Stand with Jensen” campaign, backed by Silicon Valley executives including Elon Musk.

Then, on Monday, the board said it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

“This is an extraordinary development, and the burden falls on Nvidia’s board, not on Washington. The board reinstated its CEO before the investigations into Megaspeed and his ties to it have concluded,” Shiva Rajgopal, Kester and Byrnes professor and chair of the Accounting Division at Columbia Business School, told Al Jazeera.

“For the chip industry, the lesson is that knowing your customer (KYC) is now a board-level issue. Much of the risk sits with intermediaries, especially in cloud providers and resellers in places like Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.”

Chaos at Nvidia seemed to offer immediate opportunities for competitor chipmakers such as AMD and Broadcom.

Shares in AMD, which competes directly with Nvidia in AI processors through its Instinct accelerator range, and Broadcom, which designs custom AI chips and networking technology for major cloud companies, gained nearly 6 percent on November 12, the day Huang’s departure was announced.

After Huang’s return, their shares rose modestly higher – by approximately 7 percent and 2 percent, respectively – compared with Nvidia’s 31.5 percent surge.

Alphabet, which develops its own Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), had also stood to benefit as companies such as Google and Amazon may have sought to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.

Another loser in the Trump administration appears to be the president’s national security adviser and secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a known China hardliner.

Earlier, The Washington Post had reported that Rubio set in motion the chain of events that eventually led to Huang’s removal from the board at Nvidia.

Rubio was cornered on Monday, as he appeared alongside Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the Department of State, by questions being shouted at him about Huang’s reinstatement. He did not respond to any of them.

Washington, however, added Megaspeed to its trading blacklist on Monday, hours after Huang returned to Nvidia.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed the Singapore-based company and six other firms in Southeast Asia on its Entity List.

Megaspeed and the other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, stated in a filing to the Federal Register.

articles.title: 'The View' host Ana Navarro says talk of Democrats running a 'White man' in 2028 'p---es me off'
articles.summary: Ana Navarro said on her "Bleep!" podcast that calls for Democrats to nominate a White man in 2028, even from former Harris supporters, frustrate her.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Ana Navarro said on her podcast Monday that listening to people call for the Democratic Party to nominate a White man for president in 2028 "p---es" her off, particularly after hearing it from supporters of former Vice President Kamala Harris. Navarro discussed recent politics with actors Anthony Anderson and Cedric the Entertainer on her "Bleep! with Ana Navarro" podcast when the topic switched to considering women in power in the United States. "There's all this talk of whether Kamala Harris should run again or should not run again," Navarro said. "And I hear people saying, 'No, this time we've got to nominate a White man,' because — I think people are scarred from the fact that two very qualified women, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, lost against the most unqualified human being that has ever set foot in the Oval Office." JOY BEHAR REJECTS KAMALA HARRIS FOR 2028, TELLS 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS THEY'RE NOT LIVING IN 'REALITY' She continued, "But it p---es me off to hear that said, and I'm hearing it from women, and I'm hearing it from Black women, and I'm hearing it from feminist women and liberal women who supported Kamala, who supported Hillary." Anderson asked Navarro whether she believed that the U.S. would ever elect a woman president. Though Navarro said she wasn't sure, she argued that Democrats should keep trying for the sake of potential female candidates. 'THE VIEW' GUSHES OVER HILLARY CLINTON'S WOULD-BE 2016 VICTORY SPEECH: 'SHE DID WIN' "I don't want to tell little Black girls and little Brown girls that they are out of the game from the start just because of the color of their skin or their gender. So, if they're qualified, hell yes, I want them to run and there can be a primary," Navarro said. She pointed to other countries, such as Mexico, that elected a woman as their president despite having a "less progressive" culture than the U.S. and resolved that there would someday be a female U.S. president, though she could not be sure if it would be in her lifetime. FORMER FIRST LADY JILL BIDEN DOUBTS SHE'LL SEE A WOMAN PRESIDENT IN HER LIFETIME Navarro and her fellow "The View" co-hosts discussed the idea of a female president on the show last year. Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin also disagreed with the idea that America wasn't ready for a female president. "I don't think that we're not ready. I think when you look at the two candidates that were Democratic nominees, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, there is sexism that plays in. They were flawed candidates," Griffin said. articles.title: The Timms review into Pip disability benefits - key takeaways
articles.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has published his review of the personal independence payment (Pip), along with recommended changes.
articles.body:
A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence".

The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales.

The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled.

This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign.

While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review.

The review recommends both short and long term changes

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.

The review does not propose benefits cuts

The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.

The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.

Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

How does this report sit with the Milburn review that was published last week?

Alan Milburn's report - which proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK - recommended that Pip be removed from people under 25 as part of a package of measures to tackle youth unemployment.

Today's review does not make the same recommendation. It will be up to the government to decide how they marry the two reports. They have said they are committed to reforming the Pip assessment process, but what that means in practice probably won't be known until the New Year when they publish their considered response.

articles.title: Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn
articles.summary: The party says the move could fund the construction of modern purpose-built prisons elsewhere.
articles.body:
London's Victorian jails should be closed down and the land sold off to property developers, the Conservatives have said, as they launched a plan to massively increase prison places in England and Wales.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said the move could raise £1.4bn to help fund the construction of "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere".

He claimed a Tory government would create 50,000 extra prison places within "six or seven years" and end Labour's early release scheme in its first term in office.

Labour said nobody would believe the Tory plan "given they only added a dismal 500 places while in government".

Speaking at a press conference in Westminster, Timothy said it was "fair" to highlight the previous Conservartive government's failure to significantly increase prison places.

But he insisted "this is a different generation of Conservative politicians under Kemi [Badenoch]'s leadership, and we are making different choices".

Unlike previous Tory-led administrations, they were being "explicit" about which departmental budgets they would cut - international aid, culture and the Cabinet Office - to fund new prisons, he added.

Under the Tory plans, an extra £2bn a year would go to the Ministry of Justice to pay for what Timothy called "the largest prison-building programme in modern history".

"It will let us end Labour's early release schemes once and for all, and bring back shorter sentences to lock up criminals like shoplifters," he added.

He told the audience "prison works" because it kept criminals off the street and he was "deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation".

The Conservatives are setting up a commission, chaired by former minister Sir Simon Clarke, to work out how to speed up the building of new prisons by removing obstacles in the planning, procurement and judicial systems.

The review would also look at "how to get out of the old Victorian prison estate, starting in London," Timothy said in his speech.

Prisons such as Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville "sit on some of the most valuable land in the world," he added.

"Getting out of these sites is not only a good idea in itself. It will free up land for residential use in London, where our housing shortage is most acute."

He said the Tories would "strip back regulations, like affordable housing quotas and listed status, to give the land its highest realisable value," but it would only sell off the land when "market conditions are favourable to the taxpayer".

This could raise more than £1.4bn which would go towards building new prisons "in addition to" the 50,000 places the party has already pledged to build , he added.

The previous Conservative government set out plans to sell off London's Victorian jails, but this was ditched by Boris Johnson's administration in 2019 because of the shortage of prison places.

A Labour spokesperson said: "When it comes to leaving the prisons estate on the verge of collapse, the Tories are guilty as charged.

"They should be apologising to victims of crime who they badly let down rather than spending time lecturing others who are fixing the mess they left behind."

The Labour government was "delivering the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era so victims of crime get the justice they deserve," they added.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Saurav Das on Tuesday accused the Centre of trying to suppress the youth-led movement by restricting its leaders' travel, curbing protests and censoring social media content, a day after he was stopped from travelling to the UK to attend an event at the University of Oxford.Addressing a press conference, Saurav alleged that the government was raising questions about discrepancies in his passport after immigration authorities prevented him from travelling to London.He claimed that the Centre, unable to find grounds to act against CJP leaders through agencies such as the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), was questioning their citizenship, Aadhaar cards and educational qualifications."They are now raising questions about discrepancies in my passport. They cannot find anything against any of their so-called leaders and since they cannot use UAPA, ED or CBI against us, they are resorting to such petty tactics. If I were Nirav Modi or Mehul Choksi, a red carpet would have been rolled out for me instead. As you all know, I was supposed to travel to London, but unfortunately, that could not happen because of this cowardly government," he said.Taking a swipe at the government, Saurav said that had he been fugitive businessmen Nirav Modi, Vijay Mallya or Mehul Choksi, he would have received preferential treatment and been able to leave for London within hours."Had I been Nirav Modi, Vijay Mallya, or Mehul Bhai Choksi, what would have happened to me? The visit was also expected to include engagements with students at the London School of Economics, Cambridge University, Edinburgh University and Queen Mary University."The invitation from the Oxford Union was the primary reason for my visit. Ratna was also invited. Indian students studying there wanted to understand what the CJP movement is all about. I wanted to go there and share my perspective on how such a large-scale movement evolved into a non-violent movement. There is considerable interest among Gen Z communities in several countries around the world to understand this," he said.Saurav said he had planned to speak about the movement's non-violent character and the principles of Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and B R Ambedkar."I would have talked about Gandhiji, Nehruji, Ambedkarji. I would have talked about the principles of Gandhiji, non-violence, peace, peaceful protest," he said.He questioned why the government was afraid of the movement and said the visit would have provided an opportunity to explain how a large-scale campaign could remain peaceful."I want to ask, why is this government so afraid? articles.title: Severe Thanksgiving storms threaten millions of travelers nationwide and Macy’s Day parade
articles.summary: Heavy rain and strong winds in the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day will not make travel difficult and dampen the holiday season kickoff, but also put the famed Macy’s parade in jeopardy.
articles.body: Heavy rain and strong winds in the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day will not make travel difficult and dampen the holiday season kickoff, but also put the famed Macy’s parade in jeopardy. Intense wind gusts could ground the stars of the show as they fly overhead down Manhattan for the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade’s 100th anniversary. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference that his office would be keeping an eye on the “cherished tradition.” Wind gusts of 30 to 45 mph are in the forecast. But the city says the balloons cannot fly in winds greater than 34 mph. The parade has a storied history of making it work when the weather has other plans, but this year’s plan will ultimately be a game-time decision. Two storms are converging in the Southeast on Tuesday, bringing thunderstorms, heavy rain and strong winds to the region. It will continue to move up the coast throughout the week. On Wednesday, parts of the Southeast and the mid-Atlantic will get hit by the storm with rain, winds and thunderstorms. Thanksgiving Day will bring heavy rain across the Midwest and the Northeast, with a potential wintry mix in some Midwest areas. It starts with rain in New York, Pittsburgh and Indianapolis on Thursday morning around 9 a.m. Winds will continue to increase throughout the Northeast all day. By the afternoon and evening, the storm will move over Cleveland, Buffalo and New England. Meanwhile, wintry weather could appear in the Mississippi Valley and upstate New York. Isolated rainfall totals up to 5 inches are expected in some areas. Flooding is possible from Wilmington up to Boston. Coastal flood watches are also in place for Thanksgiving Day along the East Coast. Perhaps most concerning are the winds. Wind gusts over 50 mph are forecast throughout the Northeast. Downed trees and power outages are to be expected. On the West Coast, California is also bracing for flooding this holiday week. Officials have warned people to limit their travel Tuesday and Wednesday. High tides, storm surge, rainfall and winds could cause intense flooding, officials said. Travel hit by weather, outages The weather will also affect more than 81 million people expected to travel this week to reach their holiday destinations. In recent weeks, technology outages and staffing issues have caused major ground stops at individual airports and airlines, as well as across the nationwide air travel system. As recently as Monday, Chicago O’Hare Airport issued a ground stop due to staffing constraints. It was unclear how these issues and outages might affect the busy travel week. On Wednesday, weather is likely to cause delays at airports in Miami, Orlando, Raleigh-Durham and Charlotte in North Carolina, and Atlanta. If you’re traveling on Thanksgiving Day, expect delays at airports in Washington, Boston and Chicago. Of those expected to travel, more than 72 million will get to their destination by car, according to motor club AAA. High gas prices could make this the most expensive Thanksgiving on record for those traveling by road. Major interstates in the Northeast, such as I-95 and I-80, are expected to be backed up due to the deluge.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition condemns ‘terrorist attack’ on tower in Riyadh
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition says building in financial district targeted, marking second time in a week.
articles.body:
A tower in Riyadh’s financial district has been struck by an unspecified projectile amid attacks on Saudi infrastructure by Yemen’s Houthi group, also known as Ansar Allah.

In a post on the social media platform X, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition called the Tuesday strike targeting the King Abdullah Financial District a “cowardly terrorist attack”, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.

The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh damaged the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The strike caused “material damage”.

The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.

A fourth witness told the news agency AFP that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.

No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.

articles.title: The photographs from Gaza that Sarajevo took home
articles.summary: From a photography exhibition to a weekly vigil reading out the names of killed children, solidarity grows in Sarajevo.
articles.body:
Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina – A mother holds her daughter, trying to shield and comfort her at the same time. It is the eyes you notice first. And something aches deep inside you, especially if you come from Sarajevo, a city that survived a siege by Serb forces from 1992 to 1995.

Then you remember that you are still in Sarajevo, where there is peace now.

The image is the work of Salah Ostaz, who is still in Gaza, where rockets are falling and food and water are scarce, and where the silence of most world leaders may ring louder than the explosions, even as people in the streets around the world are raising their voices.

I have been a journalist for a long time. I took my first steps as a reporter in wartime Sarajevo: front lines, massacres, morgues, mass graves, hospitals, empty markets, cultural events that people risked their lives to attend for some semblance of normality. I wrote about all of it and thought nothing could get to me any more.

Another photograph. A girl’s eyes, wide open, as though she were looking back over the past three years at everything she has seen, which I do not even want to imagine.

In the next photograph, people line up for a spoonful of food.

And then something altogether different – children smiling and swimming at dusk off a crowded beach, as if this were the happiest time of their lives. There is hope in that picture.

That is what the people who organised Ostaz’s exhibition in Sarajevo believe. I went over to ask them how it came about.

Valida Hadzimuratovic, a radio journalist and DJ known in Los Angeles as Valida Carroll, was in Sarajevo when Ostaz video-called her in October last year. Alongside other activists, she had been organising weekly TikTok livestreams in which Palestinian journalists spoke about what they had witnessed. That call was the beginning of a friendship. Over the following months, she shared his photographs and learned more about his life, including why he had not been able to collect his diploma.

“I remember thinking how frustrating it must be to finish your studies, put in all that work, and then not be able to get hold of something as basic as your own diploma,” Valida told me.

She and her friend Nasiha, a Bosnian who also lives in Los Angeles, began raising money to cover his tuition fees. In September, they decided to show Ostaz’s work in Sarajevo. He sent them more than 150 photographs. Milomir Kovacevic, who documented life in his own city during the siege of Sarajevo, helped curate the show to include about 60.

A silent auction was held alongside the exhibition, with about two dozen artisans and small businesses donating work and prizes. Volunteers and activists from the Ka Gazi (Towards Gaza) movement helped organise the event.

Every Tuesday evening, Ka Gazi volunteers gather in central Sarajevo at the Eternal Flame, an antifascist memorial commemorating those who died resisting fascism during the Second World War. They read aloud the names of Palestinian children who have been killed. If you pass by, you hear the name of one child, then another.

Last year, the names were also read at Sarajevo’s MESS International Theatre Festival. The year before, the festival opened with Metro Gaza, a production featuring the Palestinian Freedom Theatre from Jenin, in the occupied West Bank. That year’s motto was “Unstoppable Life”.

“No one who lived through the siege of Sarajevo should be indifferent to the suffering of others,” said MESS director Nihad Kresevljakovic, while visiting the photography exhibition.

At the end of the evening, people walked out of the Bosnian Cultural Centre carrying photographs and items they had won at the auction. All the proceeds went towards covering the costs of getting Ostaz his diploma.

“We can’t help everyone in Gaza. The needs are enormous and the destruction is immeasurable. But we can help one person,” Hadzimuratovic said.
